article1.title: WHY DO WE FEAR THE WRONG THINGS?
vocab: Many tourists [[perceive]] the old city as unsafe at night, although crime there is actually very low.
Engineers calculated the [[probability]] of the bridge failing in a major earthquake.
She still has [[vivid]] memories of the storm that destroyed her grandparents’ house.
For weeks before the operation, he lived with a constant sense of [[dread]].
Investors often [[overestimate]] their ability to predict how the market will move.
After ten years without an accident, the factory managers had become [[complacent]] about safety.
Experienced nurses often make [[intuitive]] decisions that turn out to be remarkably accurate.
The city built new flood barriers to [[mitigate]] the effects of heavy rain.
definitions: (adj) too satisfied with a situation, so that you stop paying attention to possible dangers
(n) how likely it is that something will happen
(v) to make something less harmful, serious or unpleasant
(v) to notice or understand something in a particular way
(adj) producing very clear, powerful images in the mind
(v) to think that something is larger, more likely or more important than it really is
(adj) based on feelings or instinct rather than on facts or careful reasoning
(n) a strong feeling of fear about something that may happen
paragraphs: Ask a nervous passenger why they grip the armrest during take-off, and they will rarely mention statistics. Measured by distance travelled, commercial flying is one of the safest ways to get from one place to another — far safer than the car journey to the airport. Yet millions of people [[perceive]] it as more dangerous than driving, and some refuse to fly at all. This gap between the risks we face and the risks we fear is not a sign of stupidity; it reflects the way the human mind evolved to make quick decisions in a world without spreadsheets or safety reports.

Psychologists have long argued that we judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. A plane crash is reported around the world for days, complete with [[vivid]] images of wreckage and grieving families, while the thousands of people who die on the roads each year rarely make the headlines. Because dramatic events are easy to picture, we tend to [[overestimate]] how often they happen, and to underestimate the slow, quiet dangers that never become news. Shark attacks, lightning strikes and terrorist incidents all loom far larger in the imagination than in the mortality tables.

Certain kinds of risk seem to trigger a particularly strong reaction. Researchers use the term ‘[[dread]] risk’ to describe low-probability events that could kill many people at once, such as a nuclear accident or a new epidemic. Such risks feel uncontrollable and unfamiliar, and people often demand far greater protection from them than from everyday hazards that, over time, claim many more lives. Control matters too: drivers tend to feel safer than passengers partly because their hands are on the wheel, even though being in charge does little to change the odds of a collision.

Misjudging risk is not merely an academic curiosity; it can have serious consequences. After the attacks on the United States in September 2001, many Americans chose to drive rather than fly for months afterwards. One widely cited study estimated that the extra traffic may have led to around 1,500 additional road deaths in the following year — far more than the number of people killed on board the hijacked planes themselves. By avoiding a frightening but rare danger, people unknowingly exposed themselves to a familiar and much more common one.

Familiarity, in fact, is one of the main reasons we underrate everyday hazards. A large share of serious accidents happen at home — on the stairs, in the kitchen or in the bathroom — yet few people think of their own house as a dangerous place. The same is true of habits such as driving while tired, eating badly or never exercising: because the harm builds up slowly and nothing bad happened yesterday, we become [[complacent]]. A risk we have survived a thousand times simply stops feeling like a risk at all.

Numbers, unfortunately, do not always help. Many people find [[probability]] difficult to interpret, especially when it is expressed as a percentage. A headline announcing that a medicine ‘doubles the risk’ of a side effect sounds alarming, but if the original risk was one in ten thousand, doubling it still leaves the chance extremely small. Without knowing the starting point, readers have no way of judging whether the change matters, and frightening relative figures can lead patients to abandon treatments that would actually do them good.

None of this means we should ignore our feelings. Our [[intuitive]] sense of danger often serves us well, warning us away from a dark alley or an unstable cliff edge long before we could calculate anything. The challenge is to recognise when instinct is likely to mislead us and to check it against the evidence. Experts suggest that presenting risks in simple terms — ‘three people in a thousand’ rather than ‘0.3%’ — can [[mitigate]] some of these biases, helping people to fear a little less of what is rare and a little more of what is common.

article2.title: WHY DO SOME PEOPLE CHASE DANGER?
article2.intro: The sentences below are about risk-taking. Choose the correct meaning (a, b or c) for the word in bold.

vocab.q: Many climbers describe reaching the summit as the most [[exhilarating]] moment of their lives.
options: extremely exciting and enjoyable
physically exhausting
deeply frightening

vocab.q: Psychologists link a love of fast cars, travel and loud music to a trait called [[sensation-seeking]].
options: a habit of avoiding strong feelings
a need for new and intense experiences
a tendency to care about others’ feelings

vocab.q: The judge described the driver’s behaviour as [[reckless]] and irresponsible.
options: carefully planned
simply unlucky
showing no thought for danger or consequences

vocab.q: Professional free divers take only [[calculated]] risks, after months of training.
options: carefully considered in advance
very small and unimportant
completely unnecessary

vocab.q: Her [[meticulous]] preparation meant that nothing was left to chance.
options: rushed and last-minute
very careful and detailed
unusually expensive

vocab.q: After his second business failed, he started a new [[venture]] selling handmade furniture.
options: a hobby done in free time
a long holiday
a new business activity that involves risk

vocab.q: Losing their biggest client was a serious [[setback]] for the small company.
options: something that delays progress or makes a situation worse
an unexpected success
a formal legal agreement

vocab.q: Athletes with great [[resilience]] bounce back quickly from injuries and disappointments.
options: physical strength
the ability to recover quickly from difficulties
natural talent

paragraphs: Every year, thousands of people pay large sums of money to throw themselves out of aeroplanes, climb frozen waterfalls or ski down slopes so steep that a single mistake could be fatal. To many observers, such behaviour looks [[reckless]], even selfish, since rescue teams and hospitals often bear the cost when things go wrong. Yet those who take part in extreme sports rarely describe themselves as careless. Instead, they talk about focus, freedom and the [[exhilarating]] sense of being completely alive — feelings they say they cannot find anywhere else in modern, comfortable life.

Psychologists have tried for decades to explain why some people actively seek out danger while others avoid it at all costs. One influential idea is [[sensation-seeking]], a personality trait describing the need for new, varied and intense experiences. People who score highly on this trait tend to become bored easily and may be drawn not only to dangerous sports but also to travel, unusual food and loud music. Research suggests that the trait is partly inherited, and that it typically peaks in late adolescence before gradually declining with age.

However, the stereotype of the adrenaline junkie who cares nothing for safety may be misleading. Interviews with experienced mountaineers, BASE jumpers and big-wave surfers reveal people who are, if anything, obsessed with control. They study weather patterns, check equipment repeatedly and rehearse emergency procedures until they become automatic. Their preparation is [[meticulous]] precisely because they understand how little room for error there is. In their own eyes, they are not gambling with their lives but taking [[calculated]] risks, reducing the danger as far as possible before deciding whether the uncertainty that remains is acceptable.

Interestingly, very similar language is used by entrepreneurs. Starting a business is rarely life-threatening, but it can put savings, careers and relationships on the line, and a large proportion of new firms close within their first five years. Successful founders often insist that they are not natural gamblers. Before launching a [[venture]], they test their ideas on small groups of customers, keep their costs low and plan what they would do if things went wrong. Like climbers, they try to limit the downside while leaving room for a potentially large reward.

What both groups seem to share is an unusual relationship with failure. A climber who turns back a few hundred metres from the summit, or a founder whose first company collapses, may treat the experience as useful information rather than as a disgrace. Studies of serial entrepreneurs suggest that an early [[setback]] can prove valuable, provided that people reflect honestly on what went wrong. This kind of [[resilience]] — the capacity to recover, adapt and try again — may matter far more in the long run than raw courage or talent.

None of this means that risk-taking is always admirable. Overconfidence has killed experienced climbers and bankrupted talented business people, and luck plays a larger role in many success stories than the winners like to admit. Still, the lives of those who deliberately court danger raise an uncomfortable question for the rest of us. In a society that increasingly tries to remove every possible hazard, we may be losing opportunities to discover what we are capable of — and to learn that most fears, once faced, are smaller than they first appeared.

Do you think extreme athletes and entrepreneurs really share the same attitude to risk? Give examples.

grammar.title: Mixed and inverted conditionals
grammar.intro: Conditionals do not always follow the neat ‘first, second, third’ patterns taught at lower levels. Mixed conditionals link a condition in one time frame to a result in another, while inverted conditionals replace *if* with *had*, *should* or *were* to create the more formal, emphatic style typical of academic and official writing.
grammar.rules_intro: The rules below show how to combine different time frames and how to form inverted conditionals correctly.

rules.rule: **Past condition → present result:** *If* + past perfect, *would* + infinitive. Use it when an earlier action (or lack of it) affects the situation now.
rules.example: If she had taken out travel insurance, she wouldn’t be paying the hospital bill herself now.

rules.rule: **Present condition → past result:** *If* + past simple, *would have* + past participle. Use it when a permanent quality or situation explains a past event.
rules.example: If he were a more cautious person, he would never have invested all his savings in one start-up.

rules.rule: **Had** + subject + past participle replaces *if* + past perfect (third or mixed conditional).
rules.example: Had I known the ice was so thin, I would never have walked across the lake.

rules.rule: **Should** + subject + infinitive replaces *if* in the first conditional. It sounds formal and suggests the situation is fairly unlikely — common in instructions and notices.
rules.example: Should you experience any chest pain, stop exercising immediately and inform a member of staff.

rules.rule: **Were** + subject + *to* + infinitive (or **Were** + subject + adjective/noun) replaces *if* in the second conditional.
rules.example: Were the government to raise the speed limit, the number of accidents would almost certainly increase.

rules.rule: **Were it not for** / **Had it not been for** + noun = ‘if something didn’t exist / hadn’t happened’. In inverted conditionals the negative is never contracted (*Hadn’t I known…* ✗).
rules.example: Had it not been for the safety rope, the climber would have fallen more than fifty metres.

academic.subtitle: Hedging and boosting — showing how certain you are
academic.skill_text: Hedging means using tentative language — *may*, *might*, *tend to*, *appear to*, *is likely to*, *it could be argued that* — so that a claim is not stated more strongly than the evidence allows. Boosting does the opposite: *clearly*, *undoubtedly*, *there is strong evidence that* show confidence when the evidence is solid. Good academic writers balance the two, hedging speculative ideas and boosting well-established facts.
example: Extreme sports are dangerous, and young people who do them are addicted to adrenaline.
Some extreme sports may carry a considerably higher risk of injury, and it could be argued that certain participants tend to seek out intense physical sensations.

blocks.text: Read the following text for questions 30-35.

blocks.title: Australia’s flying foxes are ‘curious, gentle and intelligent’ – and often misunderstood
paragraphs: *Endangered spectacled flying foxes and vulnerable grey-headed flying foxes are ‘astonishing’ animals but misinformation is rife.*

One of the most spectacular sights at Adelaide’s Womadelaide music festival is not on the official lineup. As dusk approaches, thousands of grey-headed flying foxes begin chattering and stretching their wings as they prepare to ascend from their roosts in Botanic Park and set out in search of food. “It’s an amazing sight,” says associate professor Wayne Boardman, a wildlife veterinarian and flying fox researcher at the University of Adelaide. At first a few early birds take to the skies, he says, then more and more, “diving, swooping, flapping”. “As the night sky darkens, steadily the full camp take to the air – a mass of circling, squawking bats all eager to start foraging after a day of rest.”

For many festivalgoers, the nightly fly-out ritual is their first time seeing the animals, also called megabats, up close. Boardman runs a “bat tent” near one of the main stages, kitted out with displays, videos and binoculars to educate visitors and address misconceptions about the flying foxes. “They are just astonishing animals,” he says. “The loveliness of flying foxes, their sheer beauty, astonishing biology, the amazing anatomy – it never ceases to amaze me.” Yet misinformation about the animals is rife, from well-meaning parents telling children they use sound waves to navigate (they don’t), to more sinister notions including that the animals are “pests” that “don’t belong here”. “They came of their own volition,” Boardman says. Grey-headed flying foxes first arrived in Adelaide in 2010, establishing a permanent camp on First Creek, in parklands just north of the CBD, where they have increased in number from 1,000 to about 50,000 today.

Flying foxes are nomadic, capable of travelling up to 50km at night in search of food resources such as flowering gums, figs and fruit trees. Tim Pearson, a wildlife ecologist who specialises in flying fox behaviour and communication, says the “double whammy” of destroying native forests while providing alternative food sources in farms and residential areas creates the potential for human-bat conflict and harassment, identified as a threat in recovery plans for endangered spectacled flying foxes and vulnerable grey-headed flying foxes. Populations of both species have declined in recent decades, although assessing their current status has become more challenging since the national flying fox monitoring program concluded in 2022. “The Australian attitude towards wildlife has always been positive, providing it doesn’t inconvenience you,” Pearson says. Unfortunately for flying foxes, in their case it often does.

Things have been getting better, Pearson says, but flare-ups still occur when practical concerns – about noise, the animals’ impact on fruit growers, power outages or potential disease threats – are reported in breathless terms by the media. Efforts to disperse the bats are generally counterproductive and attempts to promote empathy and coexistence have not worked. Scientists now think “normalising” flying foxes might be a way forward, depicting them as a natural part of Australian wildlife in art, photography, books, community events and education. Despite their often visible and audible presence in cities and towns, representations of flying foxes in mainstream media and popular culture remain scarce and largely negative, according to the paper published in Australian Zoologist. Pearson, a co-author of the paper, works with tame education flying foxes at a wildlife park. Once people see these cute, furry animals up close, they realise they are “curious, gentle, intelligent” with individual personalities, he says.

Doug Gimesy, a wildlife and conservation photojournalist, says bats – flying foxes and microbats – make up nearly 20% of all mammals, but “don’t get 20% of the air time”. “As a group, they’re often ignored, under-appreciated and misunderstood,” he says. “At worst they’re vilified and face a constant battle of disinformation, hate speech and are even persecuted.” Gimesy began photographing flying foxes in 2016 and has since spent more than 160 days in the field, taking thousands of images that document every aspect of their lives. Through his award-winning photographs and children’s book, Life Upside Down, Gimesy is hoping to show people how magnificent the animals are, “to get people to engage and ask questions and understand”. Two images have been important to capture and share, he says. In one, a flying fox pokes its pink tongue into a eucalyptus blossom – because people don’t realise what important pollinators they are, he says.

In the other, a pup clings to its mum as it breastfeeds in mid-flight, which usually triggers an emotional response. It’s the realization “they carry their young in flight, and they’re flying mammals”. The paper says shifting attitudes towards species such as sharks and crocodiles, once subject to widespread persecution, offer optimism that contentious issues between flying foxes and people can be managed without maligning them as a species. In Fisher reserve, in the inner Melbourne suburb of North Fitzroy, children play on the green grass as an oversized flying fox takes wing with a magpie, a squirrel glider and pink paper planes against a purple sky. The colourful mural, by Alex Sugar, is one of several depicting flying foxes alongside other Australian wildlife and quirky elements. Sugar is fond of the bats, and they became a recurrent feature in his work after their nightly flyout over the Yarra River drew his attention. “We need to highlight them more in everyday culture and the issues that they’re going through as well with their current habitat,” he says.

writing.task_intro: You are writing an essay for an academic audience. Write 180–200 words.
writing.task: Some people believe that children today are overprotected and should be allowed to take more risks in order to learn and develop. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
plan: paraphrase the question + state your position clearly
main reason(s) for your view + a specific example
concede the opposing view — which risks are not acceptable?
summarise your position in new words; do not add new ideas
rules: Answer the question that is actually asked — ‘To what extent…?’ requires a clear position, not just a list of points.
Aim for 180–200 words in four paragraphs; going far over or under the limit costs marks.
Paraphrase the question in your introduction instead of copying it word for word.
Support every main idea with a reason and a concrete example.
Hedge claims you cannot prove (may, tend to, it could be argued) and boost well-established facts (clearly, there is strong evidence).
Show a range of grammar — for example, a mixed or inverted conditional — and use formal linking words.
writing.sample:
In recent years, there has been growing concern that children are being raised in an environment so carefully controlled that they rarely face any danger at all. I largely agree that young people should be given more freedom to take sensible risks, as this is likely to make them more confident and capable adults.
Firstly, it could be argued that children learn to judge danger only by experiencing it. A child who climbs a tree and slips tends to understand height and balance far better than one who has only been warned about them. Were parents to remove every challenge, children might never develop this practical judgement. Moreover, there is strong evidence that independent play builds resilience, since minor failures teach young people that setbacks can be overcome.
Admittedly, some risks are simply not worth taking. Busy roads, deep water and the darker corners of the internet present real dangers that children cannot be expected to assess alone, and adults clearly have a duty to protect them.
In conclusion, while sensible supervision remains essential, I believe that overprotection may do more harm than good. Had my own parents not let me make small mistakes, I would probably be far more anxious today.
writing.practice_task: Some people argue that governments should protect people from the consequences of their own risky choices, for example by banning dangerous sports or taxing unhealthy food. Others believe adults should be free to take whatever risks they choose. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.

speaking.title: SPEAKING PART 3
speaking.statement: People should take more risks in life.
for: Risk-taking leads to personal growth and new opportunities
Most innovators and successful entrepreneurs took big chances
Playing it safe can lead to regret and a narrow, predictable life
against: Unnecessary risks can cause injury, debt or harm to others
Not everyone can afford to fail — the consequences are unequal
Careful planning often achieves more than bold gambles
speaking.sample:
Personally, **I’m largely in favour of** the idea that people should take more risks, although **I’d add an important condition**: the risks need to be thought through.
**The main argument in favour is that** growth rarely happens inside our comfort zone. Moving to a new city, changing careers or starting a business are all frightening, but they’re also how people discover what they’re capable of. **A good example is** my cousin, who left a stable job to open a small café. Had she stayed where she was, she’d probably still be wondering ‘what if’. **On top of that**, many of the inventions we rely on today exist only because someone was willing to fail in public.
**On the other hand, it’s worth bearing in mind that** not everyone can afford to take chances. Someone with savings and a supportive family can bounce back from a failed venture, whereas a person supporting three children may lose everything. **There’s also the point that** some risks — like dangerous driving — put other people in danger, not just the risk-taker.
**All things considered, I’d say that** people should take more calculated risks, not reckless ones. Weighing up the odds, having a back-up plan and knowing when to walk away seem to me just as important as courage.
